all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: lighting
concepts.definition: Lighting is a stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline that assigns color to a constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

concepts.name: graphics processing unit
concepts.definition: Graphics processing unit (GPU) is a parallel hardware component of a graphics card, with its own memory, that speeds up the rendering process by exploiting the inherent parallelism of graphics operations.

defining_facts.text: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).
A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process.

In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.

A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.

The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.
Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.
The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.
In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

concepts.name: Unity scene
concepts.definition: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application and is composed of game objects. Unity provides a scene interface to create, edit, or modify it.

defining_facts.text: The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.
The Unity game view is the final view used to preview a developed scene, and it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.

A Unity asset is any item used in a Unity project to create an application, can represent visual or audio elements such as three-dimensional (3D) models or textures, and examples of Unity assets are scenes, animations, materials, scripts, and prefabs.
A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.
A Unity project can contain any number of Unity scenes, depending on how many levels or layers it has, and Unity provides a scene interface to create, edit, or modify a scene.
A Unity prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object, and it allows the user to make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.

concepts.name: platform
concepts.definition: A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.
In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

concepts.name: light source
concepts.definition: A light source is an element that emits light that falls on a surface point directly or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

defining_facts.text: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.
In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface.
In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

concepts.name: application programming interface
concepts.definition: Application programming interface (API) is a predefined set of functions provided by a library that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks, allowing a programmer to deal with lower-level tasks without needing to know every detail of the underlying system or platform.

defining_facts.text: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.
The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks.

The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application.

concepts.name: native rendering library
concepts.definition: A native rendering library is a software library that sits above an operating system and provides graphics APIs that a virtual reality or game engine calls to perform rendering, rather than the developer accessing it directly.

defining_facts.text: A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

In a layered virtual reality (VR) system, a developer can rely on the software development kit (SDK) layer to access the VR engine; the developer has to install the VR engine and import the SDK within the engine, and the VR engine's job is to let the developer deal with graphics through the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by the native rendering libraries without directly accessing those native rendering libraries.

concepts.name: point of interest
concepts.definition: Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.

defining_facts.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.
In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.
For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.
A point of interest (POI) in the Satra graph does not have to refer to an actual physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.

When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.
The maximum wait time at a point of interest (POI) is the time a user needs to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

concepts.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) computer graphics pipeline (3D graphics pipeline) is a stage-wise process of computation starting from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

concepts.name: Unity
concepts.definition: Unity is a popular cross-platform game engine and developer environment that provides an editor interface and implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, enabling developers to create, build, and deploy 2D and 3D interactive content, including XR experiences.

defining_facts.text: Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.
The Unity platform comprises the Unity three-dimensional (3D) game engine and a developer's interface that a developer can use to implement ideas.

The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline.
Unity is a cross-platform game engine that Unity Technologies initially released in 2005.

Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

The Unity developer environment is an implementation platform with an editor interface through which a developer can create, build, and deploy a system, and it provides support for building an XR experience.

concepts.name: color
concepts.definition: Color is an observed combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display and mixed in the eye.

defining_facts.text: Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.

concepts.name: light intensity
concepts.definition: Light intensity is the strength of light reaching a point or the viewer’s eye, which determines the perceived color of a surface point; in the simple lighting model it is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities and typically diminishes with distance from the light source.

defining_facts.text: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point.

In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

concepts.name: graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: Graphics pipeline is the set of distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

defining_facts.text: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

concepts.name: world coordinate system
concepts.definition: The world coordinate system is the common reference frame in which all scene points are defined and to which objects are transformed from local coordinate systems to construct the scene.

defining_facts.text: The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.
The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.

The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

concepts.name: viewing pipeline
concepts.definition: The Viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the 3D graphics pipeline that selects a portion of a 3D scene and transforms it from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system through viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.
The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is view transformation, which is also called the viewing pipeline.

The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.
The sequence of stages or sub-stages in the viewing pipeline is not fixed, because different implementations can alter the sequence.
View transformation, also called the viewing pipeline, is an important stage in the 3D graphics pipeline.
Unity supports view transformation through its camera concept; after a developer sets up a camera, Unity performs the other calculations automatically.

concepts.name: mesh
concepts.definition: Mesh is a basic boundary representation technique in computer graphics that represents a three-dimensional object's surface as connected polygons, usually triangles, and stores the vertices and connections needed to reconstruct it.

defining_facts.text: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.
In mesh representation, a greater number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces but makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained.

Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.
A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.

In Unity, three-dimensional (3D) meshes are the main graphics primitives, and Unity supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes, meaning meshes whose polygons are triangles or quadrangles.
In Unity's mesh rendering workflow, the mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape.

In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

concepts.name: reflection coefficient
concepts.definition: A reflection coefficient is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light intensity reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye. In the simple lighting model, the ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients range from 0.0 to 1.0, where values near 0.0 are dull and values near 1.0 are shiny.

defining_facts.text: The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.
The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

Each of the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model has a value from 0.0 to 1.0, where a value close to 0 represents a dull surface with no reflection because most of the light is absorbed, a value close to 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface where all light gets reflected, and varying the coefficients generates different effects between dull and shiny surfaces.

concepts.name: unity editor interface
concepts.definition: The Unity editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics pipeline.

defining_facts.text: Unity Hub is a standalone application that is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine; installing Unity Hub gives the Unity Editor interface and the Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects and installations.

The Unity Editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment (IDE) whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics (CG) pipeline.
Unity Hub installation is not mandatory; the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine can be installed separately, and in that case the developer can deal with only one version of Unity.

concepts.name: game object
concepts.definition: Game object is a fundamental object in Unity that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement its functionality, so its properties are given by adding components.

defining_facts.text: A Unity game object is a fundamental object that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement the object's functionality, so its properties are given by adding components to it.

Built-in component types can be assigned to Unity game objects through the Unity editor interface, and custom components and game objects can be created using scripting application programming interfaces (APIs).
Cube, sphere, capsule, cylinder, and plane are primitive object types that can be created directly within Unity as Unity game objects.
A Unity prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object, and it allows the user to make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.

concepts.name: component
concepts.definition: A Component is a Unity asset that can be added to a game object to implement part of the object's functionality or properties, and can be a built-in component type or a custom component created by scripting.

defining_facts.text: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.

A Unity game object is a fundamental object that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement the object's functionality, so its properties are given by adding components to it.

Built-in component types can be assigned to Unity game objects through the Unity editor interface, and custom components and game objects can be created using scripting application programming interfaces (APIs).

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: Three-dimensional space is the space with x, y, and z axes in which an object can have three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.

never_defined.name: geometry
never_defined.definition: Geometry is part of a virtual environment, and, together with terrain, it affects cybersickness; in a mesh rendering workflow it is what a mesh renderer takes from a mesh filter and renders at a position defined by a transform component.

never_defined.name: camera
never_defined.definition: A camera is a sensor or component that captures or renders a view and can provide data for tracking.

never_defined.name: point
never_defined.definition: A point is a position in a coordinate system, represented by coordinates or a vector, that can be transformed between coordinate systems and mapped to integer pixel-grid coordinates for display.

never_defined.name: force
never_defined.definition: Force is a parameter associated with moving body parts that joints can apply to move rigid bodies and with which surfaces in synthetic virtual worlds interact.

never_defined.name: gravity
never_defined.definition: Gravity is one stimulus for the balance sense and what makes dropped objects accelerate toward the ground in virtual-world physics.

never_defined.name: collision
never_defined.definition: Collision is the intersection of two or more bodies in a virtual world, and a collision response determines how the bodies should behave after it occurs.

never_defined.name: surface
never_defined.definition: Surface is a boundary of an object that can be polygonal or curved.

never_defined.name: open graphics library
never_defined.definition: Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) is a native graphics library and rendering API that provides software abstractions of a graphics processing unit (GPU) for performing rendering.

never_defined.name: vulkan
never_defined.definition: Vulkan is one of the rendering application programming interfaces that provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit.

never_defined.name: animation
never_defined.definition: Animation is computer graphics content or an asset used for creating the perception of motion and in representing objects or complex characters.

never_defined.name: sound effects
never_defined.definition: Sound effects are auditory effects generated for a virtual reality system to support the desired level of sound perception.

never_defined.name: resource requirement
never_defined.definition: Resource requirement is the technological optimization concern of an XR system, which is generally resource-hungry and whose resource requirements are minimized without compromising the immersive experience.

never_defined.name: polygon
never_defined.definition: A polygon is a geometric shape used in a polygonal mesh to approximate an object's boundary.

never_defined.name: triangle
never_defined.definition: A triangle is a polygon that most graphics systems use to form meshes approximating object surfaces in rendered scenes.

never_defined.name: pipeline stage
never_defined.definition: A pipeline stage is a part of a 3D graphics or render pipeline.

never_defined.name: local coordinates
never_defined.definition: Local coordinates are the coordinates from which objects or vertices are transformed or transferred to world coordinates in rendering and scene creation.

never_defined.name: high-end graphics workstation
never_defined.definition: A High-end graphics workstation is a high-end platform with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support that is typically used for render pipelines requiring a good amount of resources.

never_defined.name: view transform
never_defined.definition: View transform is a part of the render pipeline that render pipeline support helps implement.

never_defined.name: shader
never_defined.definition: A shader is one of the elements of a render pipeline.

never_defined.name: world scene
never_defined.definition: World scene is a form of environment creation in a render pipeline, specifically world-coordinate-system scene creation.

never_defined.name: world-coordinate-system scene creation
never_defined.definition: World-coordinate-system scene creation is a type of environment creation included in the render pipeline.

never_defined.name: sky
never_defined.definition: Sky is a special environment that is part of environment creation in a render pipeline.

never_defined.name: visual effect
never_defined.definition: Visual effect is a part of render pipeline support and can be applied to the camera, game objects, light sources, and other elements of a game.

never_defined.name: pre-built render pipeline
never_defined.definition: A Pre-built render pipeline is a render pipeline provided by Unity, rather than a custom render pipeline created using Unity's scriptable render pipeline APIs.

never_defined.name: built-in render pipeline
never_defined.definition: Built-in render pipeline is one of Unity's pre-built render pipelines, with limited customization options.

never_defined.name: custom render pipeline
never_defined.definition: A Custom render pipeline is a render pipeline that can be created by a developer using Unity's scriptable render pipeline APIs.

never_defined.name: scriptable render pipeline application programming interface
never_defined.definition: Scriptable render pipeline application programming interface is an application programming interface that a developer can use to create a custom render pipeline.

never_defined.name: high-end platform
never_defined.definition: A high-end platform is, for example, a high-end graphics workstation with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support, for which a high-definition render pipeline is typically meant.

never_defined.name: animation data
never_defined.definition: Animation data is data in a model file that is included when the object represented by the file is an animated character.

never_defined.name: model file format
never_defined.definition: Model file format is a standard or proprietary format for models that can be imported into Unity and made to work.

never_defined.name: fbx file format
never_defined.definition: Fbx file format is one of the model file formats supported by Unity for importing models.

never_defined.name: dae file format
never_defined.definition: Dae file format is one of the model file formats that Unity supports for importing models.

never_defined.name: dxf file format
never_defined.definition: The Dxf file format is a model file format.

never_defined.name: obj file format
never_defined.definition: The Obj file format is a model file format that can be imported into Unity.

never_defined.name: graphics primitive
never_defined.definition: A graphics primitive is, in Unity, mainly a three-dimensional mesh, with triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes supported.

never_defined.name: quadrangle
never_defined.definition: Quadrangle is a polygon used in quadrangulated polygonal meshes.

never_defined.name: mesh renderer
never_defined.definition: Mesh renderer is a renderer that takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

never_defined.name: mesh filter
never_defined.definition: A Mesh filter is a part of a mesh rendering workflow from which the mesh renderer takes geometry.

never_defined.name: transform component
never_defined.definition: Transform component is a component of a game object that defines the position used by a mesh renderer to render geometry.

never_defined.name: tiling information
never_defined.definition: Tiling information is information included in a material's description of how an object's surface should be rendered.

never_defined.name: color tint
never_defined.definition: A Color tint is a piece of information included in a material to specify how an object's surface should be rendered.

never_defined.name: roughness
never_defined.definition: Roughness is one of the aspects of a material's surface that textures can represent.

never_defined.name: terrain features
never_defined.definition: Terrain features are built-in features in the Unity editor.

never_defined.name: speedtree toolkit
never_defined.definition: Speedtree toolkit is a toolkit supported by the latest Unity version in place of the Tree Editor.

never_defined.name: light direction
never_defined.definition: Light direction is the direction of light that developers can specify for realistic lighting on game objects.

never_defined.name: light color
never_defined.definition: Light color is the color of a light that developers can specify for realistic lighting on game objects.

never_defined.name: real-time shadow
never_defined.definition: A real-time shadow is a shadow that can be rendered using shadow mapping to support realistic lighting on game objects.

never_defined.name: shadow mapping
never_defined.definition: Shadow mapping is used to render real-time shadows for realistic lighting on game objects.

never_defined.name: camera component
never_defined.definition: A camera component is a component that is added to a game object to create a camera.

never_defined.name: directx
never_defined.definition: DirectX is a major native graphics library supported by Unity, primarily in the Windows environment.

never_defined.name: windows environment
never_defined.definition: The Windows environment is the environment in which DirectX is primarily used.

never_defined.name: metal
never_defined.definition: Metal is a major native graphics library supported by Unity for Apple systems.

never_defined.name: apple systems
never_defined.definition: Apple systems are the systems for which Unity supports the Metal native graphics library.

never_defined.name: graphics application programming interface
never_defined.definition: A graphics application programming interface is an application programming interface that accesses native graphics library application programming interfaces.

never_defined.name: default graphics application programming interface
never_defined.definition: A default graphics application programming interface is a Unity graphics application programming interface that accesses native graphics library application programming interfaces.

never_defined.name: player settings editor interface
never_defined.definition: The player settings editor interface is an editor interface opened through Edit Project Settings and used to select the Player category, navigate to Other Settings, and check the AutoGraphics API option.

never_defined.name: edit project settings
never_defined.definition: Edit project settings is used by a developer to open the Player Settings editor interface.

never_defined.name: player category
never_defined.definition: The Player category is a category in Unity's Player Settings editor interface that is selected to navigate to Other Settings, where the AutoGraphics API option is checked.

never_defined.name: other settings
never_defined.definition: Other settings is a part of the Player Settings editor interface used to check the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) option.

never_defined.name: unity player build
never_defined.definition: A Unity player build is a build that, when the AutoGraphics API option is checked, includes built-in graphics APIs and uses the appropriate one at runtime.

never_defined.name: built-in graphics application programming interface
never_defined.definition: A Built-in graphics application programming interface is one of a set of graphics application programming interfaces included in a Unity player build when the AutoGraphics application programming interface option is checked, with the appropriate one used at runtime to produce the best-case scenario for a platform.

never_defined.name: character controller
never_defined.definition: Character controller is one of the essential components included in the Unity physics engine to give a realistic feeling.

never_defined.name: primitive collider
never_defined.definition: A primitive collider is a type of collider in Unity, such as a box, sphere, or capsule collider, that defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

never_defined.name: box collider
never_defined.definition: A box collider is a primitive collider in Unity that defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

never_defined.name: sphere collider
never_defined.definition: Sphere collider is one of the primitive collider types in Unity, used to define the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

never_defined.name: capsule collider
never_defined.definition: Capsule collider is one of the primitive collider types in Unity that define the shape of a game object for physical collisions.

never_defined.name: mesh collider
never_defined.definition: A Mesh collider is a type of collider in Unity that is more processor-intensive but accurate.

never_defined.name: static collider
never_defined.definition: A static collider is a thing that can be added to a game object without a rigid body component to create motionless elements of a scene.

never_defined.name: friction
never_defined.definition: Friction is one of the things configured by physics materials in Unity for a surface.

never_defined.name: bounce
never_defined.definition: Bounce is one of the things that physics materials in Unity are used to configure for a surface, along with friction.

never_defined.name: isTrigger property
never_defined.definition: The isTrigger property is used in Unity to configure a collider as a trigger, so that the collider does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.

never_defined.name: ball and socket joint
never_defined.definition: A ball and socket joint is a kind of joint used to model the realistic movement of specific objects or characters, such as hips or shoulders.

never_defined.name: skeletal joint
never_defined.definition: A skeletal joint is an example of a joint that can be used to model the realistic movement of objects or characters.

never_defined.name: joint constraint
never_defined.definition: A joint constraint is what the inbuilt support in an articulation body automatically implements, so a developer does not need to control each individual joint to make a complex figure move realistically.

never_defined.name: logical tree
never_defined.definition: A Logical tree is a representation of an articulation body in which each node is a joint and each parent-child relationship reflects mutually constrained relative motion, so the relations and relative movements of the joints define the overall articulation.

never_defined.name: parent-child relationship
never_defined.definition: A Parent-child relationship is a relationship in a logical tree of joints that reflects mutually constrained relative motion.

never_defined.name: relative motion
never_defined.definition: Relative motion is the mutually constrained motion between parent and child joints in an articulation body.

never_defined.name: animation system
never_defined.definition: An animation system is a system that supports importing, aligning, and previewing animation clips, retargeting humanoid animations, transitions and interactions between animations, and animating different body parts with different logics.

never_defined.name: animation clip
never_defined.definition: An animation clip is an animation in an animation system that can be imported, aligned, previewed, and used in transitions and interactions with other animations.

never_defined.name: character model
never_defined.definition: A Character model is a model used in humanoid animation retargeting, where animations are applied from one model to another.

never_defined.name: audio sense
never_defined.definition: Audio sense is supported in immersive experiences through dedicated components for audio perception and playback.

never_defined.name: audio perception
never_defined.definition: Audio perception is part of the support for the audio sense in immersive experiences, provided through dedicated components such as audio source, audio listener, and audio filters.

never_defined.name: playback
never_defined.definition: Playback is part of the audio sense in immersive experiences for which dedicated components are provided, including an audio source that lets an audio clip be played back when triggered.

never_defined.name: audio clip
never_defined.definition: Audio clip is a standard audio file that can be played back by a Unity audio source when triggered.

never_defined.name: mixer
never_defined.definition: A Mixer is one way a Unity audio source can be triggered to play back an audio clip.
